paragraphs.heading: What a kelp forest is
paragraphs.text: A kelp forest is a stretch of underwater sea crowded with kelp, and kelp covers a large share of the world's coastlines. The word kelp names a group of marine algae in the order Laminariales. A smaller patch of anchored kelp is called a kelp bed instead. The forests are made of brown algae and grow along temperate and polar coasts around the world. In 2007 they were also found in tropical waters near Ecuador.

paragraphs.heading: How a kelp is built
paragraphs.text: A kelp grips the seafloor with a holdfast, a root-like clump that anchors it. Unlike a true root, the holdfast does not take up nutrients and pass them to the rest of the alga. From it rises the stipe, a stalk that works as the frame for the other parts. The fronds, flat blade-like pieces branching off the stipe, are where the kelp takes in nutrients and carries out photosynthesis. Many kinds also have pneumatocysts, gas-filled bladders near the base of the fronds, which keep the kelp floating upright.

paragraphs.heading: What kelp needs to grow
paragraphs.text: Kelp needs a hard surface to hold on to, such as rock or sand, plenty of nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus, and enough light. The richest forests tend to sit where upwelling lifts cool, nutrient-rich water from the deep into the surface layer. Moving, churning water helps the fronds soak up nutrients, and clear water lets light reach deeper. In good conditions giant kelp can grow 30–60 cm upward in a single day. Nereocystis is an annual kelp, whereas Eisenia is a perennial that can live for more than 20 years.

paragraphs.heading: Where kelp grows
paragraphs.text: Kelps mostly belong to temperate and arctic seas. The northeastern Pacific, from north of San Francisco up to Alaska's Aleutian Islands, holds the most kinds, with more than 20 species. Kelp forests are unknown in tropical surface waters, and scientists think this is mainly because those warm waters carry too few nutrients. Yet one model, which matched kelp's physical needs to average ocean conditions, predicted kelp growing below the surface across the tropics, as deep as 200 m. When researchers tested it in the Galapagos Islands, they found thriving kelp forests at all eight sites they sampled, each one predicted by the model.

paragraphs.heading: Who lives in the forest
paragraphs.text: Many sea creatures use kelp forests for shelter or food, fish among them. In the North Pacific these include rockfish and many invertebrates, such as amphipods, shrimp, sea snails, bristle worms and brittle stars. Seals, sea lions, whales and sea otters are found there too, along with birds such as gulls, terns, cormorants and great blue herons. Kelp forests rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth. Together with coral reefs they cover only 0.1% of the planet's surface, yet they account for 0.9% of its primary productivity.

paragraphs.heading: When the balance breaks
paragraphs.text: People have often played a part in the decline of kelp forests. Overfishing near the shore is a particular worry, because it can free grazing animals from the checks that normally keep their numbers down, and they then overgraze the kelp. A forest can quickly turn into a barren seafloor where few species remain. Overfishing and climate change together have already all but wiped out kelp forests in vulnerable places such as Tasmania's east coast and Northern California. Marine protected areas are one response, since they can limit fishing and shield the forest from other stresses.
